analysis.one_liner: Lets U.S. corporations move offshore patents and software home without paying tax on the gains.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have given U.S. multinationals a tax break to repatriate intangible property, died in the House Ways and Means Committee with one cosponsor and never came up for a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a new rule to the tax code: when a U.S.-owned foreign subsidiary hands patents, copyrights, software, formulas, or similar valuable intangible property back to its American parent company, the transfer would be treated as if it produced no profit. That means the parent company would pay no tax on the gain from receiving the property. The stated goal is to encourage companies to move intellectual property and, with it, investment back to the United States. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in March 2021 and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Large U.S.-based multinational corporations that hold valuable intangible property — patents, software, brands, formulas — in foreign subsidiaries. Under current law, moving that property back to the U.S. parent generally triggers tax on the built-in gain; this bill would erase that tax bill. Companies in tech, pharmaceuticals, and other IP-heavy industries would benefit most, and only they have the offshore structure this bill addresses.
analysis.who_benefits_short: U.S. multinationals holding offshore patents and software

how_it_helps.text: For transfers of intangible property from a controlled foreign corporation to its U.S. parent, the property's fair market value is treated as no more than its adjusted basis, so no taxable gain is recognized on the distribution.
If any part of the distribution is not a dividend, the shareholder recognizes no gain and takes a carryover basis, wiping out the tax that would normally apply when the property moves onshore.

The bill's title states its purpose is to 'encourage the transfer of intangible property from controlled foreign corporations to United States shareholders,' i.e., to bring intellectual property home tax-free.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. taxpayers generally. Every dollar of gain that a multinational recognizes tax-free under this rule is revenue the Treasury does not collect, which must otherwise be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing. The benefit is concentrated in a small number of very large companies; the cost is spread across everyone who pays federal taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary federal taxpayers via lost revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill is a targeted tax cut for corporations with offshore intellectual property. Under current law, bringing that property home would trigger tax on the gain; the bill eliminates that liability, so its direct effect is forgone federal revenue with no offsetting provision.

Only companies with the offshore structure it addresses — controlled foreign corporations holding substantial intangibles — can use it, so the benefit goes to large multinationals in IP-heavy industries rather than to domestic firms or workers generally.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the revenue cost. The counter-argument for the bill is that current rules can discourage companies from moving IP and associated jobs to the United States; this bill removes that friction, but it does so by giving up tax revenue rather than by requiring any new domestic investment or hiring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit case is indirect: making it cheaper to repatriate intellectual property could encourage investment in the United States. But the bill requires nothing in return — no hiring, no investment, no onshoring commitment — and its direct, certain effect is that some of the largest U.S. companies pay no tax on gains from moving offshore property home. The revenue cost is real and falls on other taxpayers; the economic benefit is speculative.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2021 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Darin LaHood introduced the bill on March 18, 2021, with Rep. Drew Ferguson as its sole cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The committee held no markup and the House never voted on the bill; no further action appears in the legislative record before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, no new tax break for multinationals with offshore intellectual property was enacted, so the Treasury kept the revenue it would otherwise have forgone. The companies the bill was written for gained nothing, but lost nothing either, since the current-law rules remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury and other taxpayers; the bill died

for.name: Rep. Darin LaHood
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 18, 2021, to create a tax-free rule for repatriating intangible property.

for.name: Rep. Drew Ferguson
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members signed on during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or any action on the bill after its referral on March 18, 2021, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The only support came from two Republicans — the sponsor and one cosponsor — and the bill sat in a committee controlled by Democrats who never acted on it; no votes were ever taken.

industries.industry: U.S. multinational corporations with offshore intellectual property (tech, pharmaceuticals, IP-heavy firms)
industries.note: The bill would let them move patents, software, and other intangibles from foreign subsidiaries to their U.S. parents without recognizing taxable gain, wiping out a tax bill they would otherwise owe. The gain to these companies would come directly out of federal revenue, so their interest runs against ordinary taxpayers'.

Every tax-free repatriation under the bill would be revenue the Treasury does not collect, made up by other taxpayers or borrowing. Had the bill passed, the cost would have been spread across everyone who pays federal taxes.
